cards.q: Who became India’s third Chief of Defence Staff on 31 May 2026?
cards.n: He came after Bipin Rawat (the first) and Anil Chauhan (the second).

cards.q: Who was India’s first Chief of Defence Staff?
In which year was the post of Chief of Defence Staff created?
cards.n: It was made so that the Army, Navy and Air Force plan and fight together.

cards.q: What is the main job given to the new Chief of Defence Staff?

cards.title: Why a CDS at all
cards.body: Before **2019** each force planned on its own. The **Chief of Defence Staff** sits above the three chiefs’ level of planning so that they buy, train and fight together. The big unfinished job is the **theatre command**: one commander for one region, with soldiers, ships and planes all under him.

cards.q: Who became Chief of the Naval Staff on 31 May 2026?
cards.n: He took over from Admiral Dinesh K. Tripathi, on the same day the new CDS took over.

cards.q: Whom did Admiral Krishna Swaminathan succeed as Navy chief?
Who became Chief of the Army Staff on 30 June 2026?
cards.n: He took over from General Upendra Dwivedi.

cards.q: Whom did General Dhiraj Seth succeed as Army chief?
Who became Chief of the Air Staff on 31 October 2026?
cards.n: He took over from Air Chief Marshal A. P. Singh. The 2021 paper asked “the present Chief of Air Staff”.

cards.q: Whom did Ashutosh Dixit succeed as Chief of the Air Staff?
cards.a: Air Chief Marshal A. P. Singh

cards.title: Four chairs in five months
cards.body: **31 May 2026**: **Raja Subramani** becomes CDS and **Krishna Swaminathan** Navy chief. **30 June**: **Dhiraj Seth** takes the Army. **31 October**: **Ashutosh Dixit** takes the Air Force. Remember the order of the months: May for two, June for the Army, October for the Air Force.

cards.title: Every door, a new name
cards.body: In most years one service chief retires and the others carry on. **2026** was different. Between May and October all four top chairs of the forces changed hands. On a single day, **31 May**, a new **Chief of Defence Staff** and a new **Navy chief** walked in together. The Army followed a month later and the Air Force in the autumn. For an examiner who asked “the present Chief of Air Staff” in 2021, it was a year full of fresh questions.

cards.q: A Captain in the Navy is equal to which rank in the Army?
cards.n: The trap: a Navy Captain is far senior to an Army Captain.

cards.q: A Captain in the Navy is equal to which rank in the Air Force?
An Army Colonel is equal to which rank in the Navy?

cards.title: The Captain trap
cards.body: The word **Captain** means two very different ranks. In the **Army** a Captain is a young officer, just above a Lieutenant. In the **Navy** a Captain is equal to an Army **Colonel** and an Air Force **Group Captain**. So when a question says “Captain”, first ask: which service?

cards.q: Which Air Force rank is equal to an Army Major?
Which Navy rank is equal to an Army Major?
Which Air Force rank is equal to an Army Lieutenant Colonel?
Which Navy rank is equal to an Army Lieutenant Colonel?
Which Navy rank is equal to an Army Brigadier?
Which Air Force rank is equal to an Army Brigadier?
Which Navy rank is equal to an Army Major General?
Which Air Force rank is equal to an Army Major General?
Which Navy rank is equal to an Army Lieutenant General?
Which Air Force rank is equal to an Army Lieutenant General?
Which Air Force rank is equal to an Army General?

cards.title: The ladder in threes
cards.body: Read each step as Army, Navy, Air Force. **Major**, Lieutenant Commander, **Squadron Leader**. Lieutenant Colonel, Commander, **Wing Commander**. **Colonel, Captain, Group Captain**. **Brigadier, Commodore**, Air Commodore. Major General, **Rear Admiral**, Air Vice Marshal. Lieutenant General, Vice Admiral, Air Marshal. General, Admiral, Air Chief Marshal.

cards.q: Who is the only officer ever made Marshal of the Air Force?
Name the three honorary five-star ranks of the Army, Navy and Air Force.
cards.a: Field Marshal, Admiral of the Fleet, Marshal of the Air Force
cards.n: They sit above General, Admiral and Air Chief Marshal.

cards.q: Exercise Dharma Guardian is held between India and which country?
cards.n: Asked in 2021 and again in 2025.

cards.q: In which State was the seventh edition of Dharma Guardian held in 2026?
With which country does India hold the naval exercise JIMEX?
cards.n: JIMEX is the Navy’s; Dharma Guardian is the Army’s. Both are with Japan.

cards.q: Exercise Yudh Abhyas is held between India and which country?
Exercise Shakti is held between India and which country?
Exercise Nomadic Elephant is held between India and which country?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: Exercise AUSTRAHIND is held between India and which country?
Exercise Surya Kiran is held between India and which country?
Exercise Sampriti is held between India and which country?
Exercise Mitra Shakti is held between India and which country?
Garuda Shakti is a special forces exercise with which country?

cards.title: Neighbours by name
cards.body: **Surya Kiran**, the sun’s ray, goes to **Nepal**. **Sampriti**, harmony, goes to **Bangladesh**. **Mitra Shakti**, the strength of friends, goes to **Sri Lanka**. **Garuda Shakti**, named after the eagle of Indonesian legend, goes to **Indonesia**, whose national airline is Garuda.

cards.q: Exercise KHANJAR is held between India and which country?
Exercise DUSTLIK is held between India and which country?
Exercise KAZIND is held between India and which country?
Where was Exercise KHANJAR held in 2026?
Where was Exercise DUSTLIK held in 2026?

cards.title: Three that sound alike
cards.body: **KHANJAR** is a dagger, and it goes with **Kyrgyzstan**: K with K. **KAZIND** carries its partner in its name: **Kazakhstan** and India. **DUSTLIK** means friendship in Uzbek, and goes with **Uzbekistan**. The examiner swaps these three, so tie each to its first letters.

cards.title: Malabar begins
cards.body: The naval exercise **Malabar** started as a drill between **India and the USA**. **Japan** became a permanent member in **2015** and **Australia** joined in **2020**, making it the same four as the Quad.

cards.q: In which year did the Malabar exercise begin?
Name the four members of the Malabar naval exercise.
cards.n: The same four as the Quad, asked in 2021. France is not a member.

cards.q: Which country joined Malabar last, in 2020?
Name the four countries of the Quad.
What is the name of India’s naval exercise with France?
With which country does India hold the naval exercise SIMBEX?
With which country does India hold the naval exercise Konkan?
What is the name of the Indian Navy’s own biggest war drill?
cards.n: Asked in 2025. It stands for Theatre Level Operational Readiness Exercise.

cards.q: How is MILAN different from Malabar or Varuna?
cards.a: It is multilateral: many navies take part
cards.n: It is hosted by the Indian Navy every two years.

cards.q: Where was MILAN first held, in 1995?
In which city is MILAN now held?
cards.n: Home of the Eastern Naval Command.

cards.q: Which event was held at Visakhapatnam along with MILAN in February 2026?

cards.title: A meeting, not a match
cards.body: In **1995** the Indian Navy invited a few nearby navies to the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**. It was not a drill against one partner. It was a get-together of many, and it was called **MILAN**, “meeting”. It grew every two years. In time it moved to **Visakhapatnam**, the home of the Eastern Naval Command, and in **February 2026** it was held there along with the International Fleet Review ⟨CHECK⟩. When an option says MILAN is with one country, it is wrong.

cards.q: What type of missile is Agni?
What is the range of Agni-5?
Which is the short-range surface-to-surface ballistic missile of the same kind as Agni?
Who is called the Missile Woman of India?
cards.n: She led the Agni projects. Asked in 2021.

cards.title: What “ballistic” means
cards.body: A **ballistic** missile is pushed up by its rocket and then falls on its target like a thrown stone, rising very high on the way. **Agni** and **Prithvi** are ballistic. A **cruise** missile is different: it flies low and level, like a plane with no pilot, all the way.

cards.q: What type of missile is Pralay?
cards.n: The 2025 paper called it an air-to-surface cruise missile. That was false.

cards.q: What is the range of the Pralay missile?
Why is Pralay called quasi-ballistic?
cards.a: It can change its path in flight

cards.q: Which two countries built BrahMos together?
Which two rivers give BrahMos its name?
What type of missile is BrahMos?
cards.n: Supersonic means faster than sound.

cards.q: What is the name of India’s subsonic cruise missile?

cards.title: Two rivers in one name
cards.body: When India and Russia agreed to build a missile together, they needed a name that belonged to both. They took the **Brahmaputra**, which flows through Assam, and the **Moskva**, which flows through Moscow. **BrahMos** flies low like a plane but faster than sound, which makes it a **supersonic cruise missile**. It can be fired from land, ships, submarines and aircraft.

cards.q: What type of missile is Akash?
What type of missile is Astra?
What is the job of the Nag missile?
From which country did India buy the S-400 air defence system?
cards.n: Asked in 2021.

cards.title: Start and target
cards.body: Name each missile by where it starts and what it hits. **Agni**: land to land. **Akash**: ground to air, at enemy planes. **Astra**: air to air, one plane at another. **Nag**: at tanks. The examiner changes one of these words, so check both halves.

cards.q: Which programme gave India Agni, Prithvi, Akash, Trishul and Nag?
Who led the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme?
cards.a: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam

cards.q: Where in Odisha is the Integrated Test Range for missiles?
cards.n: Tests are also held from Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam Island, off the Odisha coast.

cards.q: What is the island off Odisha used for missile tests now called?
cards.a: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam Island
cards.n: It used to be called Wheeler Island.

cards.q: What kind of engine burns fuel in air moving faster than sound and has no moving parts?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: Under which ministry do the Central Armed Police Forces work?
cards.n: The examiner’s favourite false statement puts them under Defence.

cards.q: Which border force is under the Ministry of Defence, not Home Affairs?
In which year was the Indian Coast Guard set up?
What is SAREX, run by the Coast Guard?
cards.a: National search and rescue exercise at sea
cards.n: It was held off Paradip in 2026.

cards.title: The one that breaks the rule
cards.body: BSF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles, CRPF and CISF all work under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**. The **Indian Coast Guard**, set up in **1978**, is the odd one out: it is under the **Ministry of Defence**. If a statement puts the BSF under Defence, it is false.

cards.title: Border Security Force raised
cards.body: After the war with Pakistan, India raised the **BSF** on **1 December 1965**. It guards the borders with **Pakistan and Bangladesh** and works under the Home Ministry.

cards.q: On which date was the Border Security Force raised?
The BSF guards India’s borders with which two countries?
Which force guards the India–Bangladesh border?
Which force guards India’s border with China?
After which war was the ITBP raised?
cards.n: The 2025 paper had three statements on the ITBP.

cards.q: Which force guards the open borders with Nepal and Bhutan?
cards.n: Raised in 1963.

cards.q: Which is the oldest of the Central Armed Police Forces?
cards.n: Raised in 1835.

cards.q: Which force guards the India–Myanmar border?
In which year was the Assam Rifles raised?
In which year did the Central Reserve Police Force begin?
Which force, raised in 1969, protects airports and big industries?
Which force is known as the black cat commandos?
cards.n: Raised in 1984.

cards.title: One border, one force
cards.body: **Pakistan** and **Bangladesh**: BSF. **China**: ITBP. **Nepal** and **Bhutan**: SSB. **Myanmar**: Assam Rifles. Inside the country: **CRPF**. Airports, the Delhi Metro and factories: **CISF**. Each force was born from an event: 1962 gave the ITBP, 1965 gave the BSF.

cards.q: Where is the National Defence Academy?
cards.n: It trains cadets of all three forces together.

cards.q: Where is the Indian Military Academy?
Where is the Indian Naval Academy?
Where is the Air Force Academy?
Where is the Officers Training Academy for short service officers?
cards.n: A second one is at Gaya. The trap places it in Pune, where the NDA is.

cards.title: Pune is the trap
cards.body: The **NDA** is at **Khadakwasla, Pune**. After it, Army cadets go to the **IMA, Dehradun**, Navy cadets to **Ezhimala** and Air Force cadets to **Dundigal**. Short service officers go to the **OTA at Chennai** (and Gaya). Because Pune is famous for the NDA, the examiner likes to put the OTA there too.

cards.q: Where is the Defence Services Staff College?
Where is the College of Defence Management?
Where is the National Defence College?
Where is the Indian National Defence University coming up?
cards.n: Asked twice, in 2018 and 2021.

cards.q: Where is the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: What is India’s highest gallantry award in war?
Put the three wartime gallantry awards in order, highest first.
cards.a: Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra

cards.q: Who designed the Param Vir Chakra medal?
What is India’s highest gallantry award in peacetime?
Put the three peacetime gallantry awards in order, highest first.
cards.a: Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra, Shaurya Chakra

cards.title: Two ladders of three
cards.body: For bravery **in war**: **Param Vir**, Maha Vir, Vir Chakra. For bravery **in peacetime**: **Ashoka**, Kirti, Shaurya Chakra. Each ladder has three steps. Learn the top of each ladder first, because that is what the examiner asks.

cards.q: Who received the first Param Vir Chakra?
cards.n: In 1947, in Kashmir.

cards.q: Who is the only Air Force officer to receive the Param Vir Chakra?
cards.a: Flying Officer Nirmal Jit Singh Sekhon
cards.n: For the 1971 war. Asked in 2021.

cards.title: Alone in the sky
cards.body: In December **1971** Pakistani jets attacked the airfield at **Srinagar**. A young pilot, **Flying Officer Nirmal Jit Singh Sekhon**, took off under fire and fought several enemy aircraft at once. He was shot down and killed. He was given the **Param Vir Chakra**, and he is still the **only Air Force officer** to receive it.

cards.q: Operation Jindagi was the rescue at which tunnel?
cards.n: One of three operation names asked in 2025.

cards.q: Operation Keller was carried out against terrorists in which district?
Operation Olivia protects which animals in Odisha?
cards.n: It is the Coast Guard’s watch over their nesting beaches.

cards.q: What was Operation Brahma?
On which date did the great earthquake hit Myanmar?
What was Operation Sindoor?
cards.a: India’s strikes on terror camps after the Pahalgam attack

cards.q: On which date was Operation Sindoor carried out?
On which date did terrorists kill tourists at Pahalgam?
Which operation hunted down the Pahalgam attackers?

cards.title: Operation Sindoor
cards.body: On **22 April** terrorists killed tourists at **Pahalgam**. On **7 May** India struck terror camps across the border in **Operation Sindoor**. A later operation, **Mahadev**, hunted down the attackers.

cards.q: What was Operation Sindhu?
cards.a: Bringing Indians home from Iran during the Israel–Iran fighting
cards.n: June 2025. Thousands of Indian students were stuck.

cards.q: What was Operation Sagar Bandhu?
cards.a: India’s relief to Sri Lanka after Cyclone Ditwah
cards.n: Late 2025. The name means “friend across the sea”.

cards.q: Which cyclone flooded Sri Lanka in late 2025?
What was Operation Urja Suraksha?
cards.a: Navy escorts for oil and gas ships coming to India
cards.n: 2026, during the Strait of Hormuz crisis. “Urja” means energy.

cards.q: Which crisis led to Operation Urja Suraksha in 2026?

cards.title: A year of names
cards.body: **Brahma**: earthquake, Myanmar. **Sindoor**: strikes after Pahalgam. **Sindhu**: students home from Iran. **Sagar Bandhu**: cyclone relief, Sri Lanka. **Urja Suraksha**: oil and gas ships escorted. Most are rescue and relief, not war, and the examiner likes exactly these.

cards.title: Friend across the sea
cards.body: Late in **2025** a cyclone named **Ditwah** crossed **Sri Lanka**. Rivers burst their banks and villages went under water. India’s ships and aircraft were among the first to arrive, carrying food, medicine and rescue teams. The mission was called **Operation Sagar Bandhu**, which means “friend across the sea”. It was the fourth relief operation of a busy year that had begun with **Operation Brahma** in earthquake-hit Myanmar.

cards.title: Bombay Plan
cards.body: Eight big businessmen, among them **J. R. D. Tata** and **G. D. Birla**, wrote a plan for free India built on heavy industry, with the state helping at the start.

cards.q: Who wrote the Bombay Plan of 1944?
cards.a: Eight industrialists, among them J. R. D. Tata and G. D. Birla

cards.q: In which year was the Bombay Plan written?
Who wrote the Gandhian Plan?
cards.n: It was built around villages and small industry. Also 1944.

cards.q: Who wrote the People’s Plan of 1945?
cards.n: It put farming and the needs of the poor first.

cards.q: Who wrote the Sarvodaya Plan of 1950?

cards.title: Four plans before the Plan
cards.body: **1944**: the **Bombay Plan** of the industrialists, and the **Gandhian Plan** of **S. N. Agarwal**. **1945**: the **People’s Plan** of **M. N. Roy**. **1950**: the **Sarvodaya Plan** of **Jayaprakash Narayan**. Pair each plan with its writer: businessmen, a Gandhian, a communist, a socialist.

cards.title: Planning Commission
cards.body: Set up on **15 March 1950** by a **resolution of the Cabinet**, not by any law or Article. The **Prime Minister** was its chairman.

cards.q: On which date was the Planning Commission set up?
Who was the chairman of the Planning Commission?
Was the Planning Commission set up by the Constitution, by a law, or by a Cabinet resolution?
What did the First Five Year Plan (1951–56) stress?
Whose model did the Second Five Year Plan follow?
cards.n: It built heavy industry.

cards.q: What is the gap of three one-year plans from 1966 to 1969 called?
cards.n: It followed two wars and a drought.

cards.q: Which government adopted the Rolling Plan in 1978?
cards.a: The Janata government of Morarji Desai
cards.n: Asked in 2021.

cards.q: Which economist gave the idea of the Rolling Plan?
Which Five Year Plan introduced the Rolling Plan?
cards.n: The 2025 paper’s answer was “none of the above”. It ran 1978–80, between the Fifth and Sixth Plans.

cards.q: What does “Rolling Plan” mean?
cards.a: Targets are reviewed each year and the plan moves one year forward
cards.n: Asked in 2018.

cards.title: The plan that kept moving
cards.body: In **1977** the Janata Party came to power, and the new Prime Minister, **Morarji Desai**, did not like the old way of fixing targets for five years at a time. In **1978** his government ended the Fifth Plan a year early and tried an idea of the Swedish economist **Gunnar Myrdal**. Each year the targets would be checked again and the plan “rolled” one year forward. The **Rolling Plan** lasted only until **1980**, when the next government went back to Five Year Plans.

cards.q: When did NITI Aayog replace the Planning Commission?
In which List of the Seventh Schedule is “economic and social planning”?
cards.n: Asked in 2021.

cards.q: What does the fiscal deficit show, in plain words?
cards.a: What the government must borrow this year
cards.n: All spending minus all income other than loans.

cards.q: What fiscal deficit does Budget 2026-27 aim at?
What is the revenue deficit?
How is the primary deficit worked out?

cards.title: The chain of four gaps
cards.body: **Revenue deficit**: day-to-day spending minus day-to-day income. **Fiscal deficit**: the whole gap, the year’s borrowing. Take **interest** out of the fiscal deficit and you have the **primary deficit**. Take **grants to States for capital assets** out of the revenue deficit and you have the **effective revenue deficit**.

cards.q: How is the effective revenue deficit worked out?
cards.a: Revenue deficit minus grants to States for creating capital assets

cards.q: In which Budget was the effective revenue deficit first used?
Is “monetary deficit” a budget term?
cards.n: The 2025 paper added it as a fake fifth deficit.

cards.title: The road that was counted as waste
cards.body: The Centre sends money to the States, and the books counted all of it as day-to-day spending. But some of that money built **roads and schools**, things that last for years. Counting it with salaries and subsidies made the gap look worse than it was. So the **Budget of 2011-12** brought a new measure, the **effective revenue deficit**: the revenue deficit minus **grants for creating capital assets**.

cards.q: Under which Article is the Finance Commission set up?
How many members does the Finance Commission have?
cards.a: A chairman and four other members
cards.n: Asked in 2021.

cards.q: How often is a Finance Commission set up?
Who sets up the Finance Commission?
Who chairs the 16th Finance Commission?
Which period does the 16th Finance Commission cover?
What share of central taxes did the 16th Finance Commission give the States?
cards.n: It kept the 15th Commission’s share.

cards.q: What share did the 14th Finance Commission give the States?

cards.title: From 42 to 41
cards.body: The **14th** Finance Commission gave the States **42%** of central taxes. The **15th** cut it to **41%**, because Jammu and Kashmir became a Union Territory and no longer took a State’s share. The **16th**, under **Arvind Panagariya** for **2026–31**, kept **41%**.

cards.q: Which law keeps the government’s deficits in check?
cards.n: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003.

cards.q: Which committee reviewed the FRBM Act?
What is the RBI’s inflation target?
cards.a: 4%, with a band of 2% either side

cards.q: Which index is used to measure the RBI’s inflation target?
cards.n: Not the Wholesale Price Index.

cards.q: Who fixes the inflation target?
cards.a: The Government, after talking to the RBI

cards.q: Since which year has the RBI had a formal inflation target?

cards.title: Four, give or take two
cards.body: The RBI must keep inflation at **4%**, and anything from **2% to 6%** is allowed. The number is fixed by the **Government after talking to the RBI**, and it is read on the **CPI**, the prices a family pays in the shop. The design came from the **Urjit Patel Committee**.

cards.q: How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee have?
What is the repo rate?
cards.a: The rate at which the RBI lends to banks

cards.q: Which committee designed inflation targeting in India?
Which office makes the Consumer Price Index?
Which office makes the Wholesale Price Index?
cards.a: Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce

cards.q: The Narasimham Committee reformed which sector?
The Malhotra Committee reformed which sector?
Which committee proposed the National Stock Exchange?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: Which committee drew the poverty line that Rangarajan later redrew?

cards.title: One committee, one sector
cards.body: **Narasimham**: **banks**. **Malhotra**: **insurance**. **Pherwani**: the **National Stock Exchange**. **Tendulkar**, then **Rangarajan**: the **poverty line**. **Urjit Patel**: **inflation targeting**. **N. K. Singh**: the FRBM law. Learn them as pairs, because the examiner swaps the sectors.

cards.q: Who regulates stock exchanges in India?
cards.n: The 2025 paper asked what the RBI does not do. This is it.

cards.q: Who regulates mutual funds in India?
cards.n: Asked in 2018.

cards.q: What is the new base year of India’s GDP series, released in February 2026?
cards.n: It moved from 2011-12.

cards.q: What is the new base year of the Consumer Price Index?
Which sector gives the largest share of India’s GDP?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.title: New yardsticks
cards.body: In **February** the statistics office released a new GDP series with base year **2022-23**, replacing **2011-12**. The Consumer Price Index also moved to a new base, **2024**.

cards.q: Which two bodies built the global Multidimensional Poverty Index?
Name the three dimensions of the Multidimensional Poverty Index.
cards.a: Health, education and standard of living
cards.n: Each has equal weight.

cards.q: How many indicators does the global MPI use?
How many indicators does India’s national MPI use?
Which two indicators does India’s MPI add to the global ten?
Which body makes India’s national Multidimensional Poverty Index?
cards.n: The 2021 paper asked who measures poverty. The answer was NITI Aayog.

cards.q: From which survey does the MPI data come?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: About how many Indians left multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23?

cards.title: Poor in more than money
cards.body: A family may earn something and still be poor if the children are out of school and there is no toilet. So the **MPI** looks at **health, education and standard of living**. The global index has **10** indicators; **NITI Aayog’s** has **12**, adding **maternal health** and a **bank account**. The data comes from the **NFHS**.

cards.title: MGNREGA
cards.body: Parliament promised every rural household **100 days** of paid work a year. It became the best-known scheme in India, until a new law replaced it in December **2025**.

cards.q: How many days of work a year did MGNREGA promise?
In which year was MGNREGA passed?
Which Act replaced MGNREGA in December 2025?
cards.a: Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act
cards.n: Called VB–G RAM G for short.

cards.q: How many days of work does the VB–G RAM G Act promise?
In which month and year did Parliament replace MGNREGA?

cards.title: From 100 days to 125
cards.body: For twenty years a village family in India could ask for **100 days** of paid work a year, and the government had to give it. That was **MGNREGA**, passed in **2005**. In **December 2025** Parliament replaced it with a new law with a long name, shortened to **VB–G RAM G**. The promise grew to **125 days**. With “employment” and “poverty alleviation” both in the syllabus, the examiner is unlikely to miss it.

cards.q: Who coined the word “ecology”?
Who coined the word “ecosystem”, and in which year?
Who drew the first pyramid of numbers?

cards.title: Three words, three people
cards.body: **Haeckel** named the subject: **ecology**, the study of living things and their surroundings. **Tansley** named the unit: the **ecosystem**, in 1935. **Elton** drew its shape: the **pyramid of numbers**, with many plants at the bottom and very few hunters at the top.

cards.q: Who gave the 10 per cent law of energy flow, and in which year?
Under the 10 per cent law, how much energy passes from one food level to the next?
cards.n: The rest is lost, mostly as heat.

cards.q: Which ecological pyramid is always upright and can never be inverted?
cards.n: A pyramid of numbers or biomass can be upside down; energy cannot.

cards.title: Why the pyramid narrows
cards.body: At each step up the food chain only about **10%** of the energy passes on. Grass with 1,000 units feeds deer with 100, and the deer feed a tiger with 10. That is why there are so few top hunters, and why the **pyramid of energy is always upright**. **Lindeman** gave the law in **1942**.

cards.q: Who gave the terms alpha, beta and gamma diversity?
What does beta diversity measure?
cards.a: The change in species from one community to the next
cards.n: Asked in 2021. Alpha is inside one community; gamma is the whole region.

cards.q: What is alpha diversity?
cards.a: The variety of species inside one community

cards.q: What is gamma diversity?
cards.a: The total variety of species over a whole region

cards.title: Alpha, beta, gamma
cards.body: Stand in one pond and count: that is **alpha**. Walk from the pond into the forest and see how the species change: that is **beta**. Count everything in the whole region: that is **gamma**. Beta is the one the examiner asks, because it is about **change between** communities.

cards.q: What is the border zone between two communities called?
What are species that live mainly in the border zone between two communities called?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: What is a species found in only one region of the world called?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: What are plankton?
cards.a: Tiny living things that drift with the water
cards.n: Asked in 2018.

cards.q: Who gave the idea of the biodiversity hotspot, and in which year?
cards.n: Asked in 2021.

cards.q: How many endemic plant species must a region have to be a biodiversity hotspot?
How much of its original vegetation must a hotspot have lost?
How many biodiversity hotspots are there in the world?
Name the four biodiversity hotspots that touch India.
cards.a: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats with Sri Lanka, Sundaland
cards.n: Sundaland reaches India through the Nicobar Islands.

cards.title: Rich and in danger
cards.body: A hotspot must pass two tests. It must be **rich**: at least **1,500 endemic plants**. And it must be **in danger**: at least **70% of its vegetation lost**. **Norman Myers** gave the idea in **1988**. The world has **36**; India touches **four**.

cards.title: A list of places to save first
cards.body: In **1988** a British ecologist, **Norman Myers**, asked a hard question. There is not enough money to save every forest. Which ones should come first? His answer was the places where many plants live nowhere else and where most of the land has already been cleared. He called them **biodiversity hotspots**. The idea caught on, and the list has grown to **36**. Four of them reach into India, from the Himalaya to the **Nicobar Islands**.

cards.title: Stockholm Conference
cards.body: The first big **UN meeting on the human environment** was held in **Stockholm**. **World Environment Day, 5 June**, marks its opening day, and the UN Environment Programme was born from it.

cards.q: The Stockholm Convention of 2001 deals with what?
cards.n: Poisons such as DDT that do not break down and travel up the food chain.

cards.q: In which city was the first big UN conference on the environment held in 1972?
World Environment Day, 5 June, marks the opening of which conference?
The Minamata Convention deals with which metal?
cards.n: Asked in 2021. Minamata is a town in Japan where factory waste poisoned the sea.

cards.q: Which convention controls the movement of hazardous waste between countries?
Which convention says dangerous chemicals can be traded only with the buyer’s informed consent?

cards.title: Tie each town to one poison
cards.body: **Stockholm**: poisons that do not break down, such as DDT. **Minamata**: **mercury**. **Basel**: **hazardous waste** crossing borders. **Rotterdam**: dangerous chemicals sold only with the buyer’s **prior informed consent**. Four towns, four problems.

cards.q: The Ramsar Convention protects what?
In which country is the town of Ramsar?
In which year was the Ramsar Convention signed?
Which treaty of 1987 protects the ozone layer?
Which convention controls trade in endangered animals and plants?
cards.n: It was signed in Washington.

cards.title: Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro
cards.body: Countries signed the **UN Framework Convention on Climate Change**. The same summit gave the **Convention on Biological Diversity** and **Agenda 21**, and the rule of common but differentiated responsibilities.

cards.q: At which summit was the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change signed?
Name two other outcomes of the Rio Earth Summit besides the UNFCCC.
cards.a: Convention on Biological Diversity and Agenda 21

cards.q: What does the rule of “common but differentiated responsibilities” say?
cards.a: All must act, but rich countries must do more
cards.n: Asked in 2021. Rich countries polluted first.

cards.title: Kyoto Protocol
cards.body: Adopted at **Kyoto** on **11 December 1997**, it set targets for rich countries to cut greenhouse gases. It named **six gases** and came into force in **2005**.

cards.q: On which date was the Kyoto Protocol adopted?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: In which year did the Kyoto Protocol come into force?
How many greenhouse gases did the Kyoto Protocol name?
At which COP was the Paris Agreement made, and in which year?
What warming limit did the Paris Agreement set?
Where was COP30 held in 2025?
Where was COP31 held in 2026?

cards.title: The climate road
cards.body: **Rio 1992**: the climate convention is signed. **Kyoto 1997**: the first binding cuts, in force 2005. **Paris 2015**, COP21: keep warming **well below 2°C**. **Belém 2025**: COP30. **Antalya 2026**: COP31. A COP is the yearly meeting of the countries that signed at Rio.

cards.title: The town that gave its name to a disease
cards.body: In the 1950s the cats of **Minamata**, a fishing town in Japan, began to shake and fall into the sea. Then the people fell ill. A factory had been pouring waste full of **mercury** into the bay for years, and the fish carried it to every table. The illness became known as **Minamata disease**. In 2013 the world signed a treaty to control mercury, and it was named after the town.

cards.q: Which body publishes the India State of Forest Report?
How often is the India State of Forest Report published?
By the 2023 report, what share of India is under forest and tree cover?
Which State has the largest forest area, by the 2023 report?
cards.n: Then Arunachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.

cards.q: Which Union Territory has the highest share of its land under forest?
Which State has the highest share of its land under forest?
Name the four States that added the most forest and tree cover in the 2023 report.
cards.a: Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan
cards.n: The 2025 question. Odisha is in it.

cards.title: Largest is not densest
cards.body: By **area**, **Madhya Pradesh** has the most forest. By **share of its own land**, **Lakshadweep** leads, and **Mizoram** leads among States. For the biggest **increase**, remember **Chhattisgarh, UP, Odisha, Rajasthan**. Read the question twice: area, share or increase?

cards.title: Project Tiger
cards.body: India began **Project Tiger** to save its tigers in special reserves. The count of **2022** found **3,682** tigers, and the next result is due in **2027**.

cards.q: In which year did Project Tiger begin?
How many tigers did the 2022 count find?
How often are India’s tigers counted?
Name Odisha’s two tiger reserves.
Which was India’s 58th tiger reserve, notified in March 2025?
Which was India’s 57th tiger reserve?
Which was India’s 56th tiger reserve?
Which State has the most tiger reserves?
cards.n: Nine, after Madhav.

cards.q: Kaziranga National Park is famous for which animal?
Gir is the only wild home of which animal?
cards.n: 891 at the 2025 count.

cards.q: Dachigam National Park protects which animal?
Which national park floats on Loktak Lake?
Keibul Lamjao is the only home of which deer?

cards.title: One park, one animal
cards.body: **Kaziranga**, Assam: the **one-horned rhino**. **Gir**, Gujarat: the **Asiatic lion**. **Dachigam**, near Srinagar: the **hangul**. **Keibul Lamjao**, Manipur: the **sangai**, on floating islands of Loktak Lake. In Odisha: **Bhitarkanika** for crocodiles, **Chilika** for dolphins, **Similipal** for black tigers.

cards.title: The park that floats
cards.body: In Manipur lies **Loktak Lake**, covered with floating mats of soil and plants called phumdis. On these mats lives a deer found nowhere else on earth, the **sangai**. It walks on the soft ground with a careful step, which is why it is called the dancing deer. To save it, India made **Keibul Lamjao**, the only floating national park in the world.

cards.q: Bhitarkanika in Odisha is known for which animal?
Chilika Lake is known for which dolphin?

cards.title: Water Act and the CPCB
cards.body: Parliament passed the **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act** and created the **Central Pollution Control Board** to enforce it. Its duties over air came with the Air Act of 1981.

cards.q: Under which Act was the Central Pollution Control Board set up?
cards.a: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

cards.q: In which year was the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act passed?

cards.title: Born from water
cards.body: The **CPCB** was not made for the air. It was born from the **Water Act of 1974**, to keep rivers clean. The **Air Act of 1981** later gave it the air too. The examiner offers 1981 or the Environment Act as the parent. The answer is the Water Act.

cards.title: Environment (Protection) Act
cards.body: After the **Bhopal gas leak** of December 1984, Parliament passed a wide law that lets the Centre act on **any kind of pollution**. It is an umbrella over the older water and air laws.

cards.q: Which disaster led to the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986?
In which year was the Wild Life (Protection) Act passed?
In which year was the National Green Tribunal set up?

cards.title: The night in Bhopal
cards.body: On a December night in **1984**, a gas leaked from a pesticide factory in **Bhopal**. It spread over the sleeping city, and thousands died. India had laws for water and for air, but none wide enough for a disaster like this. Two years later Parliament passed the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**, which lets the Centre act against any kind of pollution, from any source.

cards.q: How often does the CPCB measure pollutants at each station under the air monitoring programme?
cards.n: Asked in 2021. The programme is the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme.

cards.q: With which institute did the CPCB build the Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: What does the Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index score?
How many pollutants does India’s Air Quality Index use?
How many colour bands does the Air Quality Index have?
Under the National Clean Air Programme, by how much must cities cut PM10?
Minamata disease is caused by which metal?
Itai-itai disease is caused by which metal?
Blue baby syndrome is caused by what in drinking water?

cards.title: Three poisons, three names
cards.body: **Minamata** disease: **mercury**, from fish in a poisoned bay in Japan. **Itai-itai**, “it hurts, it hurts”: **cadmium**, which makes bones soft and painful. **Blue baby syndrome**: **nitrates** in well water, which stop a baby’s blood from carrying oxygen.

cards.q: Which Act of 1853 ended the giving of Company jobs as favours?
Which committee of 1854 designed the open civil service exam?
Why could few Indians take the early civil service exam?
cards.a: It was held only in London

cards.q: Which commission of 1886 split the service into Imperial, Provincial and Subordinate branches?
In which year was the Islington Commission set up?
Put in order: Lee, Macaulay, Islington, Aitchison.

cards.title: Four bodies in order
cards.body: **Macaulay 1854**: an open exam. **Aitchison 1886**: three branches, Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate. **Islington 1912**: a fresh look. **Lee 1923**: a Public Service Commission in India, which opened in **1926**. The years climb by about thirty, then twenty-six, then eleven.

cards.q: What is the full name of the Lee Commission?
cards.a: Royal Commission on the Superior Civil Services
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: In which year was the Lee Commission set up?
In which year did India’s first Public Service Commission open?

cards.title: The first Public Service Commission
cards.body: Acting on the **Lee Commission** of **1923**, the British opened India’s first **Public Service Commission**. Under the Constitution it became the **UPSC**.

cards.q: Who called the Indian civil service the “steel frame”?
cards.n: The British Prime Minister. Sardar Patel later kept the frame and gave it a new purpose.

cards.title: The frame that stayed
cards.body: In 1922 the British Prime Minister, **Lloyd George**, told Parliament that the Indian civil service was the **steel frame** holding the whole empire up. Twenty-five years later, many Indian leaders wanted to pull it down as a tool of foreign rule. **Sardar Patel** disagreed. He told the Constituent Assembly that without a united, protected service, the new country would fall apart. So the frame stayed, and the Constitution gave its officers a shield in **Article 311**.

cards.q: Under Article 311, who cannot dismiss a civil servant?
cards.a: Any authority lower than the one that appointed him

cards.q: Under Article 311, what must happen before a civil servant is dismissed?
cards.a: An inquiry where he can defend himself

cards.q: Which Article says an officer serves at the pleasure of the President or Governor?
Which Article lets the government make service rules?

cards.title: Pleasure, then shield
cards.body: **Article 309**: the government makes service rules. **Article 310**: the officer serves **at the pleasure** of the President or Governor. **Article 311** limits that pleasure with two shields: **no dismissal by a lower authority**, and **no dismissal without an inquiry**.

cards.q: Which Article lets Parliament create a new All India Service?
cards.n: Asked in 2021 and 2025.

cards.q: What must the Rajya Sabha do before a new All India Service is created?
cards.a: Pass a resolution by a two-thirds vote

cards.q: Where is the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration?
In which year was the LBSNAA set up?
Under which department does the LBSNAA work?
cards.n: Not the Home Ministry. The police academy at Hyderabad is the one under the Home Ministry.

cards.q: Where and in which year did the Citizen’s Charter begin?
In which year did India adopt the Citizen’s Charter?
What does a Citizen’s Charter state?
cards.a: What service an office gives, and in how many days

cards.q: What is Sevottam?
cards.a: A quality management system for public services
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: Which department built Sevottam, and in which year?
cards.a: Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, 2006

cards.q: How many modules does Sevottam have?
Name the three modules of Sevottam.
cards.a: Citizen’s Charter, Public Grievance Redress, Service Delivery Capability
cards.n: Nothing in it is about staff pay.

cards.title: Seva plus uttam
cards.body: **Sevottam** joins “seva” and “uttam”: excellent service. Made by **DARPG** in **2006**, it is a **quality management system** with three modules: the **Citizen’s Charter**, **Grievance Redress** and **Service Delivery Capability**. If an option names a fourth, such as pay or training, it is the fake.

cards.q: What is CPGRAMS used for?
cards.a: Lodging public complaints online against central offices

cards.q: Which department runs CPGRAMS?
cards.a: Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances

cards.q: On which portal do government offices buy goods?
cards.n: Government e-Marketplace.

cards.q: Which platform trains government officials online?
Which app puts many government services in one place?
What is PRAGATI?
cards.a: The Prime Minister’s screen for reviewing stuck projects

cards.q: Where can a citizen keep certificates in digital form?
What was the title of the Second ARC’s first report?
cards.a: Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance
cards.n: Asked in 2021.

cards.q: What was the Second ARC’s twelfth report called?
What is Odisha’s Mo Sarkar?
cards.a: Officers phone citizens to ask how they were treated
cards.n: Begun in 2019.

cards.title: The phone call from the office
cards.body: Most people leave a government office and never hear from it again. In **2019** Odisha tried something new. Under **Mo Sarkar**, “my government”, officers pick citizens who visited a police station or a hospital and **phone them** to ask how they were treated. A rude officer could find his name in a report. It was a simple idea, built on the old promise of the **Citizen’s Charter**: the citizen at the counter should be heard.

cards.q: Which committee studied corruption in public life in 1962?
cards.n: Asked in 2021 and 2025.

cards.q: In which year was the Santhanam Committee set up?
Which body was the first child of the Santhanam Committee’s report?

cards.title: Central Vigilance Commission
cards.body: Set up on the advice of the **Santhanam Committee**, the CVC stood for decades on a government order alone. A law gave it **statutory status in 2003**.

cards.q: In which year was the Central Vigilance Commission set up?
In which year did the CVC get statutory status?
Who coined the word “Lokpal”, and in which year?
Which body first asked for a Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas in the States?
cards.n: It was led at first by Morarji Desai.

cards.title: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act
cards.body: After the public protest of **2011** and fifty years of failed bills, Parliament passed the Lokpal law. It came into force in **January 2014**.

cards.q: In which year was the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act passed?
How many Members can the Lokpal have besides its Chairperson?
What share of Lokpal Members must be judicial Members?
Can the Lokpal look into the Prime Minister?
cards.n: It cannot touch foreign relations, security, public order, atomic energy or space.

cards.q: Who was the first Chairperson of the Lokpal?
cards.n: Appointed in 2019.

cards.q: Who is the present Chairperson of the Lokpal?

cards.title: Fifty years for one word
cards.body: **1962**: the **Santhanam Committee**. **1963**: **L. M. Singhvi** coins “Lokpal”. **1964**: the **CVC**. **1966**: the first ARC asks for a Lokpal. **2013**: the Act at last. **2019**: the first Lokpal, **Justice P. C. Ghose**. The idea took half a century to reach a chair.

cards.q: Within how many days must an office answer an RTI request?
Within how long must an RTI request be answered if life or liberty is at stake?
In which year was the Right to Information Act passed?
What did the 2021 paper call the strongest control by citizens over government?
Which Article asks the State to organise village panchayats?
cards.n: It is a Directive Principle.

cards.title: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
cards.body: It found that village schemes failed because the people had no say. It proposed **three tiers**: **village panchayat, block samiti, district parishad**.

cards.q: Which committee of 1957 proposed three-tier Panchayati Raj?
Name the three tiers proposed by the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee.
cards.a: Village panchayat, block samiti, district parishad

cards.q: Where did Nehru open the first Panchayati Raj system on 2 October 1959?
Does the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee belong among civil service committees?
cards.a: No; it is a Panchayati Raj committee
cards.n: The 2025 paper wrongly listed it with civil service committees.

cards.title: A Gandhi Jayanti in Nagaur
cards.body: On **2 October 1959**, Gandhi’s birthday, **Jawaharlal Nehru** stood in **Nagaur** in the Rajasthan desert and opened India’s first three-tier Panchayati Raj. The plan came from the **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee**, which had found that village schemes failed because villagers had no say. Gandhi had dreamed of every village as a small republic. That morning, the dream got its first office.

cards.q: Which committee of 1977 suggested a two-tier Panchayati Raj?
Which committee called Panchayati Raj “grass without roots”?
Which unit did the G. V. K. Rao Committee want as the main unit of planning?
Which committee of 1986 asked for constitutional status for Panchayats?
cards.n: The same Singhvi who coined the word “Lokpal”.

cards.title: Four committees in order
cards.body: **Balwant Rai Mehta 1957**: three tiers. **Ashok Mehta 1977**: two tiers. **G. V. K. Rao 1985**: **“grass without roots”**, make the district the unit. **L. M. Singhvi 1986**: give Panchayats **constitutional status**. The last wish came true with the **73rd Amendment, 1992**.

cards.q: Which Amendment gave Panchayats constitutional status?
Which Schedule lists the subjects of Panchayats, and how many?
What share of Panchayat seats is reserved for women under the 73rd Amendment?
Which Part of the Constitution deals with Panchayats?
Which Amendment did for towns what the 73rd did for villages?
cards.n: It added the Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects.

cards.title: 73rd and 74th Amendments
cards.body: Panchayats and town bodies got **constitutional status**. Elections every five years became compulsory, **one-third** of seats went to women, and **State Election Commissions** and **State Finance Commissions** were created.

cards.title: Battle of Plassey
cards.body: **Robert Clive** beat **Siraj-ud-Daulah**, the Nawab of Bengal. The Nawab’s own commander, **Mir Jafar**, had been bought before the fight. He stood still during the battle and was made Nawab after it.

cards.q: Which Nawab of Bengal lost the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
cards.n: He was killed a few days later. So he could not have fought at Buxar, seven years on.

cards.q: Which commander betrayed Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey and became Nawab as his prize?
Who led the Company’s army at Plassey?

cards.title: The battle that was won before it began
cards.body: On 23 June 1757 Siraj-ud-Daulah brought about fifty thousand men to the mango groves of **Plassey**. Clive had about three thousand. It should not have been a fight at all. But the largest part of the Nawab’s army stood under **Mir Jafar**, and Mir Jafar had already made a deal. At noon it rained. The Nawab’s gunpowder got wet; the English had covered theirs. By evening the Nawab was running, and a trading company had a kingdom in its hands.

cards.q: Which battle of 1760 ended French hopes in India, and who won it for the British?
cards.n: He beat the French general Count de Lally. It decided the Third Carnatic War.

cards.title: How the French lost India
cards.body: The British and the French fought three **Carnatic Wars** in the south. The last one was settled at **Wandiwash in 1760**, where **Eyre Coote** beat Count de Lally. Pondicherry fell the next year. The French got it back by treaty, but only as a trading town.

cards.title: Battle of Buxar
cards.body: **Hector Munro** beat three rulers at once: **Mir Qasim** of Bengal, **Shuja-ud-Daulah** of Awadh and the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II**. Plassey was won by a trick. Buxar was won by fighting.

cards.q: Who commanded the Company’s army at Buxar in 1764?
Name the three rulers who fought the Company together at Buxar.
cards.a: Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II
cards.n: Bengal, Awadh and the Mughal emperor. Siraj-ud-Daulah is the wrong name the examiner likes to add.

cards.q: Which Mughal emperor was beaten at Buxar?
Shuja-ud-Daulah, who fought at Buxar, was the Nawab of which state?

cards.title: Why Buxar matters more than Plassey
cards.body: At Plassey the Company beat one Nawab with the help of a traitor. At **Buxar** it beat the Nawab of Bengal, the Nawab of Awadh and the **Mughal emperor** in an open fight. After Buxar nobody in north India could say no to the Company, and the emperor himself signed away the revenue of Bengal.

cards.title: Treaty of Allahabad
cards.body: One year after Buxar, the emperor **Shah Alam II** gave the Company the **Diwani** of **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**. Diwani means the right to collect the land revenue. **Clive** signed for the Company.

cards.q: What does the word “Diwani” mean?
cards.a: The right to collect land revenue

cards.q: Which treaty gave the Company the Diwani, and in which year?
The Diwani of 1765 covered which three areas?
cards.n: “Orissa” here was only a small strip near Midnapore. The British took the rest of Odisha from the Marathas in 1803.

cards.q: Which Mughal emperor gave the Diwani to the Company?
Who signed the Treaty of Allahabad for the Company?
cards.n: He had come back to India in 1765 for a second term as Governor of Bengal.

cards.title: Two masters in Bengal
cards.body: From **1765 to 1772** Bengal had a **dual government**. The Company took the revenue (the Diwani) but did none of the work of ruling. The Nawab had to keep law and order but had no money. It was Clive’s plan. **Warren Hastings** ended it in 1772.

cards.q: What name is given to Clive’s system in which the Company took Bengal’s revenue and the Nawab kept the administration?
cards.n: It ran from 1765 to 1772.

cards.q: Who ended the dual government of Bengal, and in which year?

cards.title: Permanent Settlement
cards.body: **Lord Cornwallis** fixed the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa **for ever**. The **zamindars** became owners of the land. They kept one part in eleven and paid ten parts to the Company.

cards.q: Who brought in the Permanent Settlement, and in which year?
Under the Permanent Settlement, who became the owners of the land?
Why is the Permanent Settlement called “permanent”?
cards.a: The revenue was fixed for ever

cards.q: Which official, later Governor-General himself, planned the Permanent Settlement with Cornwallis?

cards.title: The sunset law
cards.body: The Permanent Settlement was easy on the Company and hard on everyone else. A zamindar had to pay by **sunset on a fixed day**. If he was late, his estate was sold by auction. So the zamindar pressed the farmer, and the farmer had no one to press.

cards.q: Which two officers are linked with the Ryotwari system?
In which parts of India was the Ryotwari system used?
In the Ryotwari system, who paid the land tax to the government?
cards.n: There was no zamindar in between. The tax was not fixed for ever; it was revised from time to time.

cards.q: Who introduced the Mahalwari system, and in which year?
What is a “mahal” in the Mahalwari system?
cards.n: The whole village paid the tax together, through its headman.

cards.q: In which regions was the Mahalwari system used?
cards.a: North-Western Provinces, Punjab and parts of central India

cards.title: Three ways to tax the land
cards.body: The Company tried three systems. **Permanent Settlement** (Cornwallis, 1793): the zamindar pays, in Bengal. **Ryotwari** (Munro and Read): the farmer pays, in Madras and Bombay. **Mahalwari** (Holt Mackenzie, 1822): the village pays together, in the north. Ask “who pays?” and you can tell them apart.

cards.q: What word do historians use for the ruin of India’s old crafts under British rule?
cards.n: Cheap machine-made cloth from Britain came in almost free of duty, while Indian cloth was taxed heavily in Britain.

cards.q: Who put forward the “drain of wealth” theory?
cards.n: His book was “Poverty and Un-British Rule in India” (1901).

cards.title: The drain
cards.body: **Dadabhai Naoroji** said Britain was draining India. Every year money left India as salaries, pensions and profits, and nothing came back for it. He called this the **drain of wealth** and wrote it down in “Poverty and Un-British Rule in India”. R. C. Dutt made the same case later.

cards.title: The clerk who took a kingdom
cards.body: **Robert Clive** came to Madras in 1744 as a “writer”, the lowest clerk of the Company. He hated the desk. When war with the French began he changed his pen for a sword, and at **Arcot in 1751** he made his name. Six years later he won **Plassey**. He went home rich, and came back in **1765** as Governor of Bengal to take the **Diwani** from the emperor. A clerk had become the tax collector of the richest land in India.

cards.title: Regulating Act
cards.body: The first time the British Parliament stepped in to control the Company. The Governor of Bengal became the **Governor-General of Bengal**, and **Warren Hastings** was the first. A **Supreme Court** was set up at Calcutta.

cards.q: Which was the first Act of the British Parliament to control the Company’s rule in India?
Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal?
Which Act set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta?
cards.n: The court opened in 1774.

cards.q: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta?
Which Act set up the Board of Control to watch the Company from London?

cards.title: Two masters in London
cards.body: After **Pitt’s India Act (1784)** the Company had two bosses at home. The **Court of Directors** looked after trade. The new **Board of Control**, made up of ministers, looked after political matters. This “double government” lasted until 1858.

cards.title: Charter Act
cards.body: The Company lost its **monopoly of trade** with India; it kept only tea and the China trade. **One lakh rupees a year** was set aside for education. Christian missionaries were allowed to come and preach.

cards.q: Which Act ended the Company’s monopoly of trade with India?
cards.n: It kept the monopoly in tea and in trade with China for twenty more years.

cards.q: How much money did the Charter Act of 1813 set aside each year for education?
Which Charter Act first allowed Christian missionaries to work in India?

cards.title: One lakh rupees and twenty-two years
cards.body: In **1813** Parliament told the Company to spend **one lakh rupees a year** on teaching Indians. Then nobody could agree what to teach. One group, the Orientalists, wanted Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian. The other, the Anglicists, wanted English and Western science. The money lay almost unused while they argued. The quarrel ended only in **1835**, when **Macaulay** wrote his famous Minute and **Bentinck** chose English.

cards.q: Which Act turned the Governor-General of Bengal into the Governor-General of India?
Who was the first Governor-General of India?
Who was the first Law Member of the Governor-General’s council?
cards.n: The post was created by the Charter Act of 1833.

cards.q: After which Act did the Company stop trading altogether and remain only a ruler?

cards.title: Three firsts, three Acts
cards.body: **Warren Hastings** was the first Governor-General of Bengal (Act of 1773). **William Bentinck** was the first Governor-General of India (Act of 1833). **Lord Canning** was the first Viceroy (Act of 1858). The examiner swaps the three names, so learn each with its Act.

cards.q: Which Act opened the civil service to competition?
Which committee of 1854 planned the civil service examination?
Who was the first Indian to pass the Indian Civil Service examination, and in which year?
cards.n: He was an elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore.

cards.title: An exam six thousand miles away
cards.body: From **1853** anyone could sit the civil service exam. In practice an Indian had to sail to **London**, write papers in English and compete with boys from English schools. **Satyendranath Tagore** did it in **1863**. Then the rulers made it harder. **Lytton** cut the top age to nineteen. Indians asked for decades that the exam be held in India too. That wish came true only in **1922**, at Allahabad.

cards.title: Government of India Act
cards.body: After the Revolt the **Crown** took India from the Company. A new minister, the **Secretary of State for India**, sat in London with a **council of 15**. The Governor-General was also called the **Viceroy**.

cards.q: Which office was created in London by the Government of India Act, 1858?
How many members sat in the Council of the Secretary of State for India?
Who was the first Viceroy of India?
cards.n: He was also the last Governor-General under the Company.

cards.q: In which city was the Queen’s Proclamation of 1858 read out?
cards.n: Lord Canning read it on 1 November 1858.

cards.q: Which two London bodies were ended by the Act of 1858?
cards.a: The Board of Control and the Court of Directors

cards.q: Which Act first brought Indians into the law-making council?
cards.n: They were chosen by the Viceroy, not elected.

cards.q: Which Act made the first small start with elections to the councils?
cards.n: The word “election” was not used. Local bodies sent up names. Members could also discuss the budget.

cards.q: Which Act gave separate electorates to Muslims?
cards.n: It is also called the Morley–Minto reforms.

cards.q: In the Morley–Minto reforms, which post did Morley hold and which did Minto hold?
cards.a: Morley: Secretary of State. Minto: Viceroy.

cards.q: Who was the first Indian member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council?
cards.n: He joined as Law Member in 1909.

cards.title: Separate electorates
cards.body: In a **separate electorate**, Muslim voters alone chose the Muslim members. The **Act of 1909** began it. The Viceroy, **Lord Minto**, is called the father of communal electorates. The idea grew with every later Act and ended in Partition.

cards.q: Which Act brought dyarchy to the provinces?
cards.n: It is also called the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms.

cards.q: What does “dyarchy” mean?
cards.n: Provincial subjects were cut into two lists: “reserved” for the Governor’s officials and “transferred” for Indian ministers.

cards.q: In the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms, which post did Montagu hold and which did Chelmsford hold?
cards.a: Montagu: Secretary of State. Chelmsford: Viceroy.

cards.q: Which Act first gave the Centre a legislature with two Houses?

cards.title: Dyarchy in one picture
cards.body: Under the **Act of 1919** each province had two kinds of subject. **Reserved** subjects, such as police and land revenue, stayed with the Governor and his officials. **Transferred** subjects, such as education and health, went to Indian ministers. The ministers had the work but not the money.

cards.title: Government of India Act
cards.body: The longest Act the British ever wrote for India. It gave **provincial autonomy**, planned an all-India federation, set up a **Federal Court** and separated **Burma** from India. Much of our Constitution was taken from it.

cards.q: Which Act gave autonomy to the provinces?
In which year did the Federal Court begin work?
cards.n: It was set up under the Act of 1935 and sat in Delhi.

cards.q: Which country was separated from India by the Act of 1935?
Which two new provinces were made in 1936?
On which date did Odisha become a separate province?
cards.n: The day is kept as Utkal Dibasa.

cards.q: The Act of 1935 ended dyarchy in the provinces. Where did it plan to bring dyarchy instead?
cards.n: This part never came into force, because the princes did not join the federation.

cards.title: The ladder in one breath
cards.body: **1773** Governor-General of Bengal. **1784** Board of Control. **1813** trade monopoly ends. **1833** Governor-General of India. **1853** open competition. **1858** Crown rule. **1861** Indians in council. **1892** first elections. **1909** separate electorates. **1919** dyarchy. **1935** provincial autonomy.

cards.title: Delhi Durbar
cards.body: **Lord Lytton** held a grand durbar at Delhi to declare **Queen Victoria the Empress of India**. A terrible famine was killing people in the south at the same time.

cards.q: Which Viceroy held the Delhi Durbar of 1877?
What was announced at the Delhi Durbar of 1877?
cards.a: Queen Victoria was declared Empress of India

cards.q: Which Viceroy passed the Vernacular Press Act, and in which year?
Which other Act of 1878 stopped Indians from keeping weapons without a licence?
The Vernacular Press Act applied to newspapers in which languages?
cards.n: English papers were left alone. That is why it was called the “Gagging Act”.

cards.q: Lytton cut the top age for the civil service exam from 21 to what?

cards.title: Lytton’s black list
cards.body: Learn **Lord Lytton (1876–80)** as the Viceroy who made India angry. He held the **Delhi Durbar (1877)** during a famine. He passed the **Vernacular Press Act** and the **Arms Act** in 1878. He cut the civil service age to 19. Each one gave the early nationalists something to fight.

cards.title: The paper that changed its language overnight
cards.body: The **Vernacular Press Act of 1878** was aimed at Indian-language papers. The sharpest of them was the **Amrita Bazar Patrika** of **Sisir Kumar Ghosh**, printed in Bengali. The Act could not touch an English paper. So the brothers who ran it did a simple thing. The very next issue came out fully in **English**. The law had nothing to hold on to, and the paper went on scolding the government for many more years.

cards.title: Ripon’s Resolution
cards.body: **Lord Ripon** asked for local boards in towns and districts, with most members elected and not chosen by officials. For this he is called the **Father of Local Self-Government** in India.

cards.q: Which Viceroy is called the Father of Local Self-Government in India?
cards.n: The name comes from his Resolution of 1882.

cards.q: Who repealed the Vernacular Press Act, and in which year?
In which year was the first Factory Act passed, and under which Viceroy?
cards.n: It was meant to protect child workers.

cards.q: What did the Ilbert Bill of 1883 try to allow?
Who was Ilbert, after whom the Ilbert Bill is named?
cards.a: The Law Member of Ripon’s council
cards.n: His full name was Courtenay Ilbert.

cards.q: Which education commission did Ripon appoint in 1882?
cards.n: It looked mainly at primary and secondary schools.

cards.q: The first regular census of all India was taken in which year?
cards.n: A first try was made in 1872 under Lord Mayo. From 1881 it has been held every ten years.

cards.title: What the Ilbert Bill taught India
cards.body: The Europeans in India rose in anger against the **Ilbert Bill**, and **Ripon** had to weaken it. Indians watched and learnt a lesson: a noisy, organised protest can bend the government. Two years later, in 1885, the Congress was born.

cards.title: Lytton and Ripon side by side
cards.body: **Lytton** passed the Vernacular Press Act (1878); **Ripon** repealed it (1882). Lytton passed the Arms Act; Ripon passed the first **Factory Act (1881)**. Lytton held a durbar; Ripon gave **local self-government (1882)**, the **Hunter Commission (1882)** and the **Ilbert Bill (1883)**.

cards.title: Wood’s Despatch
cards.body: **Charles Wood** asked for a full ladder of schools, from the village school to the university, and for a department of education in every province. It is called the **Magna Carta of English Education in India**.

cards.q: What is called the Magna Carta of English Education in India?
Which post did Charles Wood hold when he sent his Despatch?
cards.a: President of the Board of Control

cards.q: Which three universities opened in 1857?
Who was the Governor-General when Wood’s Despatch arrived?

cards.title: Macaulay’s Minute
cards.body: **Macaulay** argued that the government’s money should go to teaching Western learning through **English**. The Governor-General, **William Bentinck**, agreed, and English became the language of higher education.

cards.q: What did Macaulay’s Minute of 1835 decide?
cards.a: English would be the language of teaching

cards.q: Which Governor-General accepted Macaulay’s Minute?

cards.title: The downward filter
cards.body: Macaulay did not plan to teach every Indian. He wanted to educate a small class in English and let knowledge “filter down” from them to the people. This is called the **downward filtration theory**. Wood’s Despatch of 1854 gave it up and asked for mass schooling.

cards.q: Put these in order of time: Sadler, Hunter, Hartog, Raleigh.
Put these in order of time: Kothari, Sargent, Radhakrishnan, Wardha scheme.
The Raleigh Commission of 1902 looked at what, and which Viceroy appointed it?
cards.n: It led to the Indian Universities Act of 1904.

cards.q: The Sadler Commission of 1917 studied which university?
By what other name is the Wardha scheme of 1937 known?
cards.n: It was Gandhi’s idea: learning through a craft, in the mother tongue. A committee under Zakir Husain worked it out.

cards.q: Which was the first education commission of free India, and in which year?
cards.n: It looked at university education.

cards.q: Which commission of 1964–66 gave the 10+2+3 pattern?
The Hartog Committee of 1929 was a branch of which larger commission?

cards.title: Eight names in a row
cards.body: The 2025 paper asked the order of the education commissions. Say it as one line: **Hunter 1882, Raleigh 1902, Sadler 1917, Hartog 1929, Wardha 1937, Sargent 1944, Radhakrishnan 1948, Kothari 1964**. The first four are British-era bodies. Wardha is Gandhi’s. The last two belong to free India.

cards.q: Which is counted as the first political association of modern India, and in which year was it founded?
cards.n: Dwarkanath Tagore was among its founders. It spoke for the zamindars of Bengal.

cards.q: Who founded the Mohammedan Literary Society in Calcutta in 1863?
Who founded the East India Association, where and in which year?

cards.title: Mr Narrow Majority
cards.body: **Dadabhai Naoroji** believed the British public would be fair if only it knew the truth about India. So he went to live among them. In **1866** he started the **East India Association** in London. In **1892** he stood for the British Parliament from Finsbury and won by a handful of votes, so few that people joked and called him “Mr Narrow Majority”. He was the **first Indian member of the House of Commons**. India called him the **Grand Old Man**.

cards.q: Who was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons?
cards.n: He won in 1892. He is called the Grand Old Man of India.

cards.q: Which association was founded at Poona in 1870, and who is the name linked with it?
cards.a: Poona Sarvajanik Sabha; M. G. Ranade

cards.title: Indian Association
cards.body: **Surendranath Banerjea** and **Ananda Mohan Bose** started it in Calcutta. It was the strongest political body before the Congress, and it led the protest when the civil service age was cut.

cards.q: Who founded the Indian Association in 1876?
cards.a: Surendranath Banerjea and Ananda Mohan Bose

cards.q: Who founded the Central National Mohammedan Association?
cards.n: He founded it in Calcutta in 1877.

cards.q: Which two associations were founded just before the Congress, in 1884 and 1885?
cards.a: Madras Mahajan Sabha and Bombay Presidency Association

cards.title: The elder brothers of the Congress
cards.body: Say them by year. **1863** Mohammedan Literary Society (Abdul Latif). **1866** East India Association (Naoroji). **1870** Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (Ranade). **1876** Indian Association (Banerjea). **1884** Madras Mahajan Sabha. **1885** Bombay Presidency Association. Then the Congress.

cards.title: Indian National Congress
cards.body: The first session met at **Bombay** in December 1885 with **72 delegates**. **W. C. Bonnerjee** was the president. A retired British officer, **A. O. Hume**, had brought the leaders together.

cards.q: Where was the first session of the Indian National Congress held, and who presided?
Which retired British civil servant helped to found the Congress?
Who was the Viceroy when the Congress was founded in 1885?
Which newspaper did Raja Rammohan Roy run?
Dadabhai Naoroji ran which newspaper?
Who founded The Hindu?
cards.n: It began in Madras in 1878.

cards.q: Who founded the Amrita Bazar Patrika?
Name Tilak’s two newspapers and the language of each.
Which two papers did Annie Besant run?
Who ran the newspaper Al-Hilal?
Who ran the newspaper Comrade?
cards.n: The examiner swaps Comrade and Al-Hilal. Comrade was English; Al-Hilal was Urdu.

cards.q: Name two newspapers that Gandhi ran in India.
cards.n: He also ran Navajivan in Gujarati, and Indian Opinion in South Africa.

cards.q: Which newspaper did Dr Ambedkar start in 1920?

cards.title: A paper and its owner
cards.body: The examiner gives a newspaper and asks the owner. Pair them: **Sambad Kaumudi** and Rammohan Roy. **Rast Goftar** and Naoroji. **Kesari** and Tilak. **New India** and Besant. **Al-Hilal** and Azad. **Comrade** and Mohammad Ali. **Young India** and Gandhi. **Mook Nayak** and Ambedkar.

cards.q: Which was the first Odia newspaper, and who started it?
cards.n: It began in 1866, the year of the great famine.

cards.q: Who started The Samaja, and in which year?

cards.title: Utkal Dipika
cards.body: **Gourishankar Ray** brought out the first newspaper in Odia from Cuttack. It began in the year of the Na’anka famine and spoke up for the Odia language and for famine relief.

cards.q: Which was the first newspaper printed in India, and in which year?

cards.title: The first editor went to jail
cards.body: India’s first newspaper was a small weekly started at Calcutta in **1780** by an Irishman, **James Augustus Hicky**. He called it the **Bengal Gazette**. Hicky printed gossip about the Company’s officers and then went after the Governor-General himself, **Warren Hastings**. He was fined and jailed, and in 1782 his types were seized. The paper lived only two years. But it set the pattern for a hundred years: Indian papers and the government were never friends.

cards.q: Which Governor-General brought in press censorship in 1799?
Who is called the Liberator of the Indian Press, and why?
cards.a: Charles Metcalfe; he removed the press curbs in 1835

cards.q: Who made a licence compulsory for every press in 1823?

cards.title: Four press laws
cards.body: **1799** Wellesley brings censorship, in fear of the French. **1823** John Adam makes a licence compulsory. **1835** Charles Metcalfe frees the press. **1878** Lytton gags the Indian-language papers. Tight, tighter, free, tight again.

cards.q: Who called Tilak the “Father of Indian Unrest”?
cards.n: He was a British journalist. He said it in his book “Indian Unrest” (1910).

cards.q: Valentine Chirol’s book “Indian Unrest” gave a famous title to which leader?

cards.title: An insult worn as a medal
cards.body: In 1910 a British journalist, **Valentine Chirol**, wrote a book to explain why India was angry. He blamed one man and called him the **Father of Indian Unrest**. **Tilak** went to London and took him to court for it. He lost the case and a great deal of money. But in India the insult was read as praise. If the British thought one man had woken the country, that man must be worth following.

cards.q: Which slogan is Tilak remembered for?
cards.a: “Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it”

cards.q: By which title, meaning “honoured by the people”, is Tilak known?
Which two festivals did Tilak turn into public gatherings?
cards.a: The Ganapati festival and the Shivaji festival
cards.n: Ganapati in 1893 and Shivaji in 1895. A religious crowd could meet where a political one could not.

cards.q: In which jail was Tilak kept from 1908 to 1914, and which book did he write there?
Tilak died on 1 August 1920. Which movement began on that same day?

cards.title: Tilak in five lines
cards.body: Newspapers: **Kesari** (Marathi) and **Mahratta** (English). Festivals: Ganapati and Shivaji. Slogan: “Swaraj is my birthright”. Jail: **Mandalay**, 1908–14, where he wrote **Gita Rahasya**. Last work: the **Home Rule League** and the **Lucknow Pact**, both 1916.

cards.q: Who were Lal, Bal and Pal?
cards.a: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal
cards.n: Punjab, Maharashtra and Bengal. They led the Extremists in the Congress.

cards.q: Bipin Chandra Pal belonged to which province?
cards.n: He edited New India and worked on Bande Mataram.

cards.title: Moderates and Extremists
cards.body: The **Moderates**, such as Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta, sent petitions and trusted British fairness. The **Extremists**, **Lal, Bal and Pal**, wanted boycott, swadeshi and mass action. The two groups broke apart at **Surat in 1907** and came together again at **Lucknow in 1916**.

cards.title: Surat split
cards.body: The Congress broke in two at its Surat session. The Moderates kept the party; the Extremists under Tilak were shut out for nine years. **Rash Behari Ghosh** was the president of the session.

cards.q: At which session did the Congress split into Moderates and Extremists, and in which year?
Who presided over the Surat session of 1907?

cards.title: Partition of Bengal
cards.body: **Lord Curzon** cut Bengal in two. He said the province was too big to govern. Indians saw a plan to divide Hindus and Muslims. The answer was the **Swadeshi movement**: boycott foreign cloth, buy Indian.

cards.q: Which Viceroy partitioned Bengal in 1905?
Which movement began as the answer to the Partition of Bengal?
In which year was the Partition of Bengal cancelled, and what else was announced with it?
cards.a: 1911; the capital would move from Calcutta to Delhi
cards.n: Lord Hardinge was the Viceroy. King George V announced it at the Delhi Durbar.

cards.q: Where and in which year was the Muslim League founded?

cards.title: Two Home Rule Leagues
cards.body: **Tilak** started his league in April, for Maharashtra and Karnataka. **Annie Besant** started hers in September from Madras, for the rest of India. Both asked for self-government inside the British Empire.

cards.q: Who started the two Home Rule Leagues of 1916?
cards.n: Tilak’s came first, in April. Besant’s followed in September.

cards.q: What did the Lucknow Pact of 1916 bring together?
cards.a: The Congress and the Muslim League
cards.n: At the same session the Moderates and Extremists also came back together.

cards.q: Who presided over the Lucknow session of 1916?
Which leader is called “Punjab Kesari”?
Which newspaper did Lala Lajpat Rai found?
Who was the first president of the All India Trade Union Congress?
cards.n: The year was 1920.

cards.q: Lala Lajpat Rai died of injuries received in a protest against what?
cards.n: The police lathi-charged the march at Lahore in October 1928. He died on 17 November.

cards.q: Which society did Lala Lajpat Rai found?
cards.n: Do not mix it up with Gokhale’s Servants of India Society (1905).

cards.title: The blows at Lahore
cards.body: On 30 October 1928 the Simon Commission reached Lahore station. A silent crowd stood there with black flags, led by an old man, **Lala Lajpat Rai**. The police charged with lathis and the blows fell on his chest. That evening he said that every blow on his body would prove a nail in the coffin of British rule. He died on **17 November**. A month later a young man named **Bhagat Singh** shot a police officer, Saunders, in revenge.

cards.q: Who founded the Servants of India Society, and in which year?
Whom did Gandhi call his political guru?

cards.title: Gandhi comes home
cards.body: Gandhi landed at Bombay from South Africa on **9 January 1915**. The day is now kept as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas. On Gokhale’s advice he spent a year travelling and listening before he spoke on Indian politics.

cards.q: On which date did Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
cards.n: The day is now Pravasi Bharatiya Divas.

cards.q: Put in order: Kheda, Champaran, Rowlatt Satyagraha, Ahmedabad Mill Strike.

cards.title: Four small fights
cards.body: Gandhi tested satyagraha four times before he used it on the whole country. **Champaran 1917**: indigo farmers. **Ahmedabad 1918**: mill workers, and his first hunger strike. **Kheda 1918**: farmers who could not pay tax. **Rowlatt 1919**: his first all-India call.

cards.q: Which was Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India, and in which year?
The Champaran satyagraha was fought for farmers forced to grow which crop?
cards.n: Under the “tinkathia” system a farmer had to grow indigo on three parts in twenty of his land.

cards.q: Champaran is in which State?

cards.title: The farmer who would not go away
cards.body: In 1916 a farmer from Champaran named **Rajkumar Shukla** came to the Lucknow Congress. He wanted someone to see how the indigo planters treated his people.
